text:
We always see the same side of the Moon because of **tidal locking**, which makes its rotation period match its orbital period. The Moon spins once on its axis in the same 27.3 days it takes to circle Earth once.

This isn't a coincidence. Early on, the Moon rotated faster. Earth's gravity raised a tidal bulge on it, and as the Moon rotated, friction within it dragged on that bulge and slowed the spin. Eventually the bulge aligned with Earth and the rotation settled to match the orbit.

Because of slight wobbles called libration, we can actually see about 59% of the surface over time. The "far side" isn't permanently dark, though. It gets sunlight just like the near side.
